title: WPMS/396/2016 of Ram Lal Vs Dr. H.k. Sharma

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHNAD AT NAINITAL
Recall Appl. No. 871 of 2017
Exemption Appl. No. 11482 of 2017
Stay Appl. No. 12180 of 2017
In
WPMS No. 396 of 2016
Ram Lal .......Petitioner
Vs.
Dr. H.K. Sharma .......Respondent
Mr. S.K. Jain, Senior Advocate assisted by Mr. Siddhartha Jain, Advocate for the
appellant.
Mr. Piyush Garg, Advocate for the respondent
Hon'ble Lok Pal Singh, J.
1. Brief facts of the case are that writ petitioner,
who is a landlord, filed a release application under
Section 21(1)(a) of U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of
Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 (hereinafter referred
to as the U.P. Act No.13 of 1972) for release of
accommodation in question after his retirement on the
ground of bonafide need of his family. The tenant
contested the release application and averred that the
landlord had entered into an agreement to sell with the
tenant and his wife and an unregistered agreement to sell
was executed between them on 13.5.1993 and in lieu
thereof huge amount was paid by the tenant and his wife
to the landlord. Learned prescribed authority at the time
of deciding the release application formulated following
two points for determination:
i) Whether the applicant has bonafide need of
the property in question and what would be
the effect of agreement to sell dated
13.5.1993?

2
ii) If, in case, the release application is allowed
or rejected which party shall face hardship?
2. Learned Prescribed Authority, after giving full
opportunity to lead the evidence to the parties and after
considering the fact that an unregistered agreement to
sell dated 13.5.1993 was executed between the parties,
recorded its finding that as the rent has not been paid to
the landlord since 1993 therefore relationship of landlord
and tenant does not exist between the parties and
decided point no.1 against the landlord. Learned
Prescribed Authority on the findings arrived at point no.1
decided the issue/point of comparative hardship in
favour of tenant and dismissed the release application by
its judgment and order dated 3.11.2010.
3. Feeling aggrieved by the said judgment and
order dated 3.11.2010, the landlord-petitioner preferred
an appeal being Rent Control Appeal No.177 of 2010. The
appellate court also recorded the same finding that
landlord and tenant relationship does not subsist
between the parties and thus there is no requirement to
decide the question of comparative hardship and
accordingly dismissed the appeal by judgment and order
dated 19.12.2015. Feeling aggrieved by the said
judgment and order, the landlord-petitioner preferred
writ petition before this Court.
4. This Court entertained the writ petition on
24.2.2016 and issued notice to the respondent-tenant
and directed the petitioner to take steps for service upon
the respondents. In compliance thereto, steps were taken
by the petitioner by both ways to serve the respondents.

3
Registered notices were sent to the respondent. Postman
visited the residence of the respondent on 08.03.2016
and again on 09.3.2016 but as the respondent was not
available at his house the postman made an
endorsement that ''recipient is not available''. Again on
10.3.2016, the postman went to serve the notice upon
the respondent and made an endorsement that ''recipient
refused to receive the notice''. Registered notice came
back with the refusal report made by postman to this
Court. This Court, in its order dated 11.5.2017, observed
that none is present for the respondent despite service of
notice. Thereafter, this case was listed several times but
hearing could not take place due to paucity of time.
Ultimately, hearing of case was taken up on 17.07.2017
and the Court proceeded ex-parte. This Court considered
the provisions of Section 35 of Stamp Act as well as the
provisions of Section 49 of Registration Act and gave its
thoughtful consideration to the provisions of Section 53-
A of Transfer of Property Act and after considering the
judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court [Deep Chandra Juenja
vs. Smt. Lajwanti Kathuria (dead) through LRs, 2008
U.A.D. 808], held that the landlord is the best judge of
his personal need and after assigning reasons, allowed
the writ petition by judgment and order dated
17.07.2017. Relevant paragraphs of the judgment are
reproduced hereunder:
"15. After considering the submissions of learned
senior counsel for the petitioner, this Court is of the
view that mere agreement to sell will not terminate
landlord-tenant relationship unless there is
stipulation to that effect in agreement itself. Unless
and until the said document is registered, it shall
have no effect for the purposes of Section 53-A of
the Transfer of Property Act. Admittedly, in the

4
present case, the agreement to sell is not registered,
therefore, the question of invocation of Section 53-A
of the Transfer of Property Act for obtaining the
possession of the property in part performance of
the contract would not arise. Notwithstanding the
agreement of sale, the relationship of landlord and
tenant continues to operate till there is a specific
agreement to end the relationship of landlord and
tenant and by merely entering into an agreement of
sale, the tenant did not acquire any right in the
property. In the present case, there is no registered
agreement to sell, there could be no reliance upon
the said document in terms of the Section 53-A of
the Transfer of Property Act. An unregistered
agreement to sell of immovable property is
inadmissible in evidence. Therefore, the findings of
two courts below regarding the effect of Section 53-
A of the Transfer of Property Act will not sustain.
16. In so far as the bonafide need and the
comparative hardship are concerned, this Court is
of the view that, in the given facts and
circumstances of the case, the landlord has been
able to make out a case of genuine bonafide need
for the premises in dispute, inasmuch as the
landlord was aged about 72 years when the
release application was filed; at present, he must
be more than 80 years old; the landlord has
specifically mentioned in the release application
that he is a retired employee of the ONGC; after
retirement, he wants to settle at Dehradun as he
has vast social circle there; he alongwith his wife
wants to settle down in their house in their old age
and desire to come back to Dehradun in the last
stage of their life as they feel lonely and insecure in
Ahmadabad; and, moreover, he (landlord) is the

5
best judge of his requirement and, therefore, this
court is not inclined to dictate him as to how and in
what manner he should live.
17. It is natural aspiration for a landlord in his
old age to stay in his own house in the evening of
his life and a desire to spend the last few years of
the life in the own house cannot be regarded as
fanciful. The findings recorded by both the
authorities that the landlord has no bonafide need
and comparative hardship is in favour of the tenant
requires to be interfered with.
18. Taking into consideration the facts and
circumstances of the case, no useful purpose will be
served by remanding the matter to the court below.
Unnecessarily, agony of the parties would be
prolonged. More than nine years have already been
elapsed and it is desirable that the controversy be
set at rest. Time upto 17.10.2017 is granted to the
respondent-tenant to vacate the disputed
accommodation, provided he files an undertaking
on affidavit within a period of one month from
today before the Prescribed Authority that he will
vacate the premises in question on or before
17.10.2017 and will handover the vacant and
peaceful possession of the premises in question,
without inducting any person therein, to the
petitioner-landlord. The tenant will pay or deposit
the entire arrears of rent and damages after
adjusting the amount, if any, already paid, due
upto 17.10.2017. In case of default of either of the
conditions stipulated above, it shall be open to the
petitioner-landlord to apply for execution of the
release order."

6
5. After the decision of this Court dated
17.07.2017, recall application being MCC No.871 of 2017
was filed by the respondent-tenant. This recall
application was listed before the same Bench, who
decided the writ petition on merits, i.e., before Justice
U.C. Dhyani. Justice U.C. Dhayni recused to hear the
recall application due to some personal reason and
directed to list the matter before another Bench and as
such this recall application has come before me.
6. The recall application has been filed by the
respondent-tenant on the ground of non-service of notice
upon him, and also that the respondent had entered into
an agreement to sell with the petitioner therefore the
tenant is entitled to get the benefit of Section 53-A of
Transfer of Property Act. It is contended that respondent-tenant only came to know about the judgment dated
17.07.2017 passed by this Court when the landlord
moved an amendment application in SCC suit No. 27 of
2016 pending between the parties in regard to the same
property in the court of District Judge, Dehradun and
sought amendment to the effect that the writ petition
filed by the petitioner-landlord has been allowed by
judgment and order dated 17.07.2017. It is also
contended that the report of refusal has been made by
the postman in connivance with the landlord.
7. Learned counsel for the respondent would
submit that the respondent was not aware about the
pendency of writ petition and the postman never
approached him to serve the notice issued by this Court.
There was no occasion for the respondent not to contest
the writ petition. Learned counsel would further submit

7
that there is concurrent findings of fact of the courts
below in favour of the tenant-respondent that
relationship of tenant and landlord does not subsist
between the parties after execution of agreement to sell
dated 13.5.1993.
8. The landlord has filed its objections to the
recall application and has stated that SCC Suit No. 27 of
2016 was filed against the applicant on 01.07.2016. In
paragraph 7 of the plaint, details of filing the present writ
petition was given. Translated version of paragraph-7 is
reproduced hereunder:
"7. That the plaintiff has filed writ petition
WPMS No.396 of 2016 Shri Ram Lal vs. Sri H.K.
Sharma in the Hon'ble High Court of Uttarakhand
at Nainital against the order dated 03.11.2010
passed by learned Prescribed Authority and order
dated 19.12.2015 passed by learned appellate
court and the Hon'ble High Court of Uttarakhand
has passed the following order in WPMS No.396 of
2016:
WPMS No. 396 of 2016
Hon'ble U.C. Dhyani J.
Mr. S.K. Jain Senior Advocate assisted by
Mr. Siddhartha Jain Advocate for the
petitioner.
Issue notice to the Respondent.
Steps be taken within a week.
List after service report is received."
9. It is also stated in the objections that on
19.10.2016 the defendant-respondent filed his written
statement. This fact about pendency of writ petition has
not been denied by the respondent/defendant in his
written statement. Moreover, against the objections to the
recall application, no reply or rejoinder affidavit has been
filed by the respondents thus the averments made in the

8
objections, which are supported by an affidavit, remains
unrebutted.
10. The burden lies upon the applicant firstly to
prove that the postman had any connivance with the
landlord and secondly that he had no knowledge of
pendency of writ petition and thirdly that there is no
inaction on his part in non-appearing to contest the
proceedings. The applicant has leveled bald allegation
that the landlord was in connivance with the postman.
Mere allegations are not sufficient, without there being
any evidence. Section 101 of Evidence Act lays burden of
proof on the party who is making allegation to prove the
same, unless the same facts are not proved by the cogent
evidence. There is hardly any occasion to believe that
there was connivance between the petitioner and
postman to get the endorsement of refusal. The applicant
has miserably failed to prove any connivance between the
landlord and the postman, thus this ground has no avail
to applicant. Averment in regard to pendency of writ
petition before this Court is admitted to the applicant.
11. For setting aside an ex-parte order 'sufficient
cause' is mandatory condition. But the applicant has
miserably failed to show any 'sufficient cause' or good
reason for setting the judgment and order dated
17.07.2017. The Coordinate Bench, after considering the
material available on record, though in absence of the
applicant, has considered the respective case of parties
and has decided the case on merit and has allowed the
writ petition.

9
12. Although, recall application was filed by the
applicant-respondent to recall the order dated
17.07.2017 but during the course of arguments learned
counsel for the applicant-respondent has vehemently
submitted that this recall application may also be
considered as review application and placed reliance
upon a decision of Hon'ble Apex Court judgment
rendered in the case of Parimal vs. Veena reported in
2011(3) SCC 545.
13. I have heard learned counsel for the parties
and have carefully perused the judgment, of which recall
has been sought, as well as Parimal's case [2011(3) SCC
545] (supra) .
14. The Hon'ble Apex Court in its celebrated
judgment Parimal vs. Veena reported in 2011(3) SCC 545
has laid down the principle of law that "sufficient cause"
is the mandatory condition to get the ex-parte order set
aside. Relevant paragraphs of the judgment are
reproduced below:-
"12. It is evident from the above that an ex-parte
decree against a defendant has to be set aside if the
party satisfies the Court that summons had not been
duly served or he was prevented by sufficient cause
from appearing when the suit was called on for
hearing. However, the court shall not set aside the said
decree on mere irregularity in the service of summons
or in a case where the defendant had notice of the date
and sufficient time to appear in the court. The
legislature in its wisdom, made the second proviso,
mandatory in nature. Thus, it is not permissible for
the court to allow the application in utter disregard of
the terms and conditions incorporated in the second
proviso herein.
13. "Sufficient Cause" is an expression which
has been used in large number of Statutes. The
meaning of the word "sufficient" is "adequate" or
"enough", in as much as may be necessary to answer
the purpose intended. Therefore, word "sufficient"
embraces no more than that which provides a

10
platitude which when the act done suffices to
accomplish the purpose intended in the facts and
circumstances existing in a case and duly examined
from the view point of a reasonable standard of a
cautious man. In this context, "sufficient cause"
means that party had not acted in a negligent manner
or there was a want of bona fide on its part in view of
the facts and circumstances of a case or the party
cannot be alleged to have been "not acting diligently"
or "remaining inactive". However, the facts and
circumstances of each case must afford sufficient
ground to enable the Court concerned to exercise
discretion for the reason that whenever the court
exercises discretion, it has to be exercised judiciously.
(Vide: Ramlal. v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd.,, Lonand
Grampanchayat v. Ramgiri Gosavi, Surinder Singh
Sibia v. Vijay Kumar Sood, and Oriental Aroma
Chemical Industries Limited v. Gujarat Industrial
Development Corporation)
14. In Arjun Singh v. Mohindra Kumar , this
Court observed that every good cause is a sufficient
cause and must offer an explanation for non-appearance. The only difference between a "good
cause" and "sufficient cause" is that the requirement of
a good cause is complied with on a lesser degree of
proof than that of a "sufficient cause". (See also: Brij
Indar Singh v. Lala Kanshi Ram Manindra Land and
Building Corporation Ltd. v. Bhutnath Banerjee
and Mata Din v. A. Narayanan).
15. While deciding whether there is a sufficient
cause or not, the court must bear in mind the object of
doing substantial justice to all the parties concerned
and that the technicalities of the law should not
prevent the court from doing substantial justice and
doing away the illegality perpetuated on the basis of
the judgment impugned before it. (Vide: State of Bihar
v. Kameshwar Prasad Singh ; Madanlal v. Shyamlal,
Davinder Pal Sehgal v. M/s. Partap Steel Rolling Mills
(P) Ltd.; Ram Nath Sao Ram Nath Sao v. Gobardhan
Sao; Kaushalya Devi v. Prem Chand; Srei International
Finance Ltd., v. Fair growth Financial Services Ltd.
and Reena Sadh v. Anjana Enterprises).
16. In order to determine the application under
Order IX, Rule 13 CPC, the test has to be applied is
whether the defendant honestly and sincerely intended
to remain present when the suit was called on for
hearing and did his best to do so. Sufficient cause is
thus the cause for which the defendant could not be
blamed for his absence. Therefore, the applicant must
approach the court with a reasonable defence.
Sufficient cause is a question of fact and the court has
to exercise its discretion in the varied and special
circumstances in the case at hand. There cannot be a
strait-jacket formula of universal application.

11
15. In the light of aforesaid, this Court finds that
the applicant, who is a highly educated person,
deliberately has not pleaded in his application that he
was not aware about the pendency of writ petition, more
particularly, when the petitioner had averred in his
plaint, which was filed on 01.07.2016 that writ petition
has been filed by the petitioner and notices have been
issued to the respondent. On 19.10.2016, written
statement was filed was filed by the respondent in the
suit and reply to this averment was given in para-12,
which is reproduced as under:
"12. That insofar as the contents of para 7 of the
plaint are concerned, it is submitted that the
defendant has no knwlodge of the institution or
filing of the writ petition by the plaintiff in the
Hon'ble High Court. The defendant has till date not
received any summons of any writ petition from the
Hon'ble High Court."

16. From the reply given in the written statement,
there is no room for doubt, that it was within the
knowledge of the respondent that writ petition is pending
before this Court. In such circumstances, it was
incumbent upon the respondent to take care of his rights
but he chose not to contest the writ petition at that point
of time. The respondent cannot make excuse of his own
wrong act. Firstly, he refused to receive the summons
and secondly despite knowing the fact that writ petition
is pending for disposal before this Court, he did not come
forward to contest the case. Even otherwise, I have also
considered the submissions of learned counsel for the
petitioner on merit. It is settled proposition of law the
landlord is the best judge of his requirement and the
tenant has no right to dictate the landlord as to how and
in what manner he should live. Perverse findings were

12
recorded by the courts below while rejecting the release
application on the ground that landlord and tenant
relationship does not subsist between the parties. It is
well settled that tenant is always a tenant unless the
tenant acquires the title over the tenanted property.
Thus, he cannot deny the relationship of tenant with the
landlord. In my considered opinion, writ petition has
rightly been allowed by the Coordinate Bench. The
applicant has miserably failed to show any "sufficient
cause" in its recall application for recall of the order
dated 17.07.2017 as well as on merit also there is no
scope of interference. I do not find any reason to recall
the judgment and order dated 17.7.2017 passed by the
Coordinate Bench. Present recall application is nothing
but absolutely abuse of process of law and has been filed
by the applicant unnecessarily to prolong the litigation.
17. Recall application is devoid of any merit and
the same is hereby dismissed.
18. At last, I could not refrain myself from saying
that the time of Court is precious and so many people are
waiting for their turn to get justice, but due to pendency
of cases and dilatory practice adopted by the litigants in
most of the cases, these litigants suffer in getting justice
in time. Now time has come to stop the dilatory tactics
adopted by the litigants or some of the lawyers.
19. In the facts of the case, parties shall bear their
own costs.
